text: What should a production plan include?
optionA: Only a list of tools needed
optionB: The stages of manufacture in sequence; materials; fittings; finishes and time allocations
optionC: A list of users who will buy the product
optionD: Only a final drawing of the finished product
explanation: A production plan details the step-by-step stages of manufacture; specifying materials; processes; fittings; finishes and estimated times for each stage.

text: What is the purpose of a working drawing in D&T?
optionA: To show a rough sketch of an idea
optionB: To provide full details for manufacture including dimensions; materials and tolerances
optionC: To advertise the finished product
optionD: To show how a product is used by the customer
explanation: A working drawing is a precise technical drawing that includes all the information a maker needs: exact dimensions; material specifications; tolerances and jointing details.

text: What is a materials list (bill of materials) used for?
optionA: To list all tools in the workshop
optionB: To specify every material and component required; with quantities and sizes; for making the product
optionC: To list the names of team members
optionD: To record test results after manufacture
explanation: A materials/components list (bill of materials) details every item needed — wood; metal; screws; paint; etc. — with quantities and dimensions; enabling accurate costing and ordering.

text: Why is it important to plan the stages of manufacture before starting?
optionA: To impress the examiner with long plans
optionB: To identify the correct order of operations; prevent mistakes; manage time and ensure efficient use of materials
optionC: To avoid having to draw anything by hand
optionD: Because CAD software requires it
explanation: Pre-planned manufacture stages prevent errors (e.g. drilling before gluing); help allocate time; ensure the correct tools are ready and reduce material waste.

text: In a production plan; what is a Gantt chart used for?
optionA: To show the cross-section of a material
optionB: To visually represent tasks over time; showing when each manufacturing stage will take place
optionC: To list the properties of different materials
optionD: To draw orthographic projections
explanation: A Gantt chart is a bar chart used in production planning to schedule tasks against a timeline; showing start/end dates and which activities overlap.

text: What does a 'specification' document do in the design process?
optionA: It tells the maker which tools to use
optionB: It lists the criteria the final product must meet; against which designs and the finished product are evaluated
optionC: It records the history of the company
optionD: It lists the names of similar products on the market
explanation: A specification is a list of measurable criteria (e.g. dimensions; weight; cost; colour; safety standards) that the final product must satisfy.

text: At what stage of the design process should production planning take place?
optionA: Before any design ideas are generated
optionB: After a final design has been selected and developed in detail
optionC: Before researching the design brief
optionD: After the product has been tested
explanation: Production planning follows design development. Once a final solution has been detailed and working drawings produced; the maker can plan how to manufacture it efficiently.

text: What is a jig used for in manufacturing?
optionA: To measure the colour of a finish
optionB: To hold or guide a tool or workpiece so that operations are repeated accurately and consistently
optionC: To clean tools after use
optionD: To calculate the cost of materials
explanation: A jig is a device that holds and guides a workpiece or cutting tool; ensuring identical operations can be repeated accurately (e.g. drilling holes in the same position on multiple pieces).

text: What should a product evaluation test?
optionA: The personal opinion of the maker without evidence
optionB: The performance of the product against each point in the original specification
optionC: The speed at which the product was made
optionD: Only the aesthetic appearance of the product
explanation: A product evaluation tests the finished product against each criterion in the specification; providing evidence (testing; user feedback) of whether each criterion has been met.

text: Which of the following is a valid method for evaluating a product's performance?
optionA: Assuming it works because it looks good
optionB: Collecting user questionnaire responses; conducting tests and comparing results to the specification
optionC: Asking only the maker whether they are satisfied
optionD: Saying it meets the specification without testing
explanation: Valid evaluation combines objective testing (measurements; functionality tests) with user feedback (questionnaires; interviews) compared against specification criteria.

text: What should a good evaluation include; besides saying what works?
optionA: Identification of weaknesses and suggestions for further development or improvement
optionB: A list of all tools used to make the product
optionC: Details of every mark scheme point from the exam
optionD: A repeat of the original design brief
explanation: A thorough evaluation identifies both strengths and weaknesses of the product; and proposes specific improvements that would address those weaknesses.

text: What is formative evaluation in a design project?
optionA: Evaluation carried out only once at the end
optionB: Ongoing evaluation throughout the design and making process to guide decisions
optionC: Evaluation done by an independent judge
optionD: Evaluation that ignores the original specification
explanation: Formative evaluation happens throughout the project (at each design and making stage) and informs decisions going forward — it is different from final (summative) evaluation.

text: A student tests their product and finds it is 2 mm too wide to fit in its intended space. What type of problem is this?
optionA: An aesthetic problem
optionB: A functional/dimensional problem — the product does not meet a specification criterion
optionC: A health and safety problem
optionD: A manufacturing cost problem
explanation: A dimensional failure means a specification criterion — a size requirement — has not been met. This is a functional/technical problem identified through measurement testing.

text: What is a user trial?
optionA: The maker testing their product alone
optionB: Giving the product to intended users to try in real or simulated conditions and gathering their feedback
optionC: A test carried out only on the materials used
optionD: A financial cost analysis of the product
explanation: A user trial involves giving the product to representative users; observing them using it and collecting their feedback; which provides real-world evidence for evaluation.

text: Why should factors such as ergonomics; aesthetics; safety and economics be considered during evaluation?
optionA: They are only considered in the design stage
optionB: They inform whether the product is truly successful and suitable for its intended users and market
optionC: They are not part of the IGCSE D&T specification
optionD: They only apply to products made from metal
explanation: A complete evaluation considers all factors from the specification: functional (ergonomics; safety); aesthetic; economic (cost) and environmental — not just whether it physically works.

text: What is a freehand sketch used for in design communication?
optionA: To produce a final technical drawing
optionB: To quickly explore and communicate initial ideas before formal drawing
optionC: To measure exact dimensions of a component
optionD: To create a finished product advertisement
explanation: Freehand sketches are used early in the design process to rapidly generate and communicate ideas; they are not precise but allow quick visual thinking.

text: What type of drawing shows an object as it would appear to a person — giving a 3D impression with parallel lines?
optionA: Orthographic projection
optionB: Isometric drawing
optionC: Pie chart
optionD: Flow chart
explanation: Isometric drawing presents a 3D view of an object on a 2D surface using lines at 30° to the horizontal; giving a realistic-looking but measurable 3D representation.

text: What is orthographic projection used for?
optionA: To show a 3D perspective view of an object
optionB: To show multiple 2D views of an object (front; side; top) with accurate dimensions for manufacturing
optionC: To show how a mechanism moves
optionD: To illustrate the colour scheme of a product
explanation: Orthographic projection (first or third angle) shows the object from multiple directions in flat 2D views with true dimensions — the standard format for manufacturing drawings.

text: What do annotations on design sketches add?
optionA: Decoration to make the page look busier
optionB: Written notes explaining materials; dimensions; construction methods or design decisions linked to the sketch
optionC: The examiner's comments on the work
optionD: A list of all previous similar products
explanation: Annotations are written notes added to sketches that explain the designer's thinking: materials; processes; dimensions; how it works; why decisions were made.

text: What is a rendered drawing?
optionA: A drawing with no colour or shading
optionB: A drawing with realistic shading; colour and texture applied to communicate the appearance and materials of a design
optionC: A technical drawing showing internal sections
optionD: A list of materials written beside a sketch
explanation: Rendering applies colour; shading and texture to a drawing to give it a lifelike 3D appearance; communicating finish; material type (shiny metal; rough wood; etc.) to viewers.

text: What is an exploded view drawing used to show?
optionA: The side view of a product
optionB: How the components of a product fit together by drawing them separated along their assembly axis
optionC: The colour scheme of a final product
optionD: The stages in a production plan
explanation: An exploded view separates components along a common axis to reveal how they assemble; often used in instructions and design presentations.

text: What advantage does CAD (Computer-Aided Design) offer over manual drawing?
optionA: It is always faster for simple shapes
optionB: It allows designs to be easily edited; scaled; rotated and viewed in 3D; and shared electronically
optionC: It removes the need for any design process
optionD: It is free to use and requires no training
explanation: CAD enables rapid editing; accurate scaling; 3D modelling; rendering; and direct data transfer to CAM equipment — advantages over manually redrawn alternatives.

text: What does CAM stand for in design and technology?
optionA: Computer-Aided Manufacture
optionB: Computer-Assisted Modelling
optionC: Computer-Activated Mechanism
optionD: Creative Artistic Method
explanation: CAD/CAM: Computer-Aided Design / Computer-Aided Manufacture. CAM uses computer data from CAD files to control manufacturing equipment such as CNC routers; laser cutters and 3D printers.

text: What does the term 'one-off production' mean?
optionA: Making products in a continuous automatic process
optionB: Producing a single unique item made to individual requirements
optionC: Making products in groups of identical items
optionD: Using only one material for the entire product
explanation: One-off (bespoke) production makes a single item tailored to specific requirements. It is typically skilled and time-consuming — examples include custom furniture; a bespoke suit or a hand-made prototype.

text: What is batch production?
optionA: Making a single unique product
optionB: Making identical products in a fixed quantity group; then possibly making a different product in the same equipment
optionC: Continuously making the same product 24/7
optionD: Using a 3D printer for every product
explanation: Batch production makes a set quantity of a product then stops. The same machinery may then be used to make a different product. Examples: a run of 500 chairs; seasonal clothing.

text: What is mass production?
optionA: Making products one at a time by hand
optionB: Continuously producing large volumes of identical products using automated production lines
optionC: Making only 10–50 of a product at a time
optionD: Producing products using only CAD software
explanation: Mass production uses automation to continuously make large numbers of identical products at low unit cost. Examples: cars; smartphones; food packaging.

text: Why is surface preparation important before applying a finish to wood?
optionA: It makes the wood stronger
optionB: It opens the grain to absorb the finish and removes blemishes; ensuring an even professional result
optionC: It prevents the wood from absorbing moisture
optionD: It converts softwood to hardwood
explanation: Surface preparation (sanding; filling; planing) removes imperfections; raises and levels the grain and ensures the finish adheres evenly and looks professional.

text: What is the purpose of a template in making?
optionA: To measure the temperature of a material
optionB: To ensure identical shapes are cut accurately and repeatedly without re-marking each time
optionC: To bend metal at a precise angle
optionD: To test whether a joint is watertight
explanation: A template is a shape guide placed on the material and drawn around (or cut along); enabling identical shapes to be reproduced accurately and efficiently.

text: What is vacuum forming used to make?
optionA: Metal car body panels
optionB: Plastic sheets formed into 3D shapes over a former by applying heat and atmospheric pressure
optionC: Composite fibre panels
optionD: Printed circuit boards
explanation: Vacuum forming heats a thermoplastic sheet until it softens; stretches it over a former and uses a vacuum to pull it tightly into shape. Used for packaging; trays; product housings.

text: Why should excess material (a machining allowance) be left on a workpiece before final finishing?
optionA: To make it cheaper to produce
optionB: To allow accurate final cuts to be made to meet the precise finished dimensions
optionC: To test the properties of the material
optionD: To allow for shrinkage during cooling
explanation: A machining allowance is intentionally left so final cuts (turning; milling; grinding) can achieve the precise finished dimensions and surface quality required.

text: What is the main difference between thermoplastics and thermosetting plastics?
optionA: Thermoplastics are always transparent; thermosetting plastics are opaque
optionB: Thermoplastics can be reheated and reshaped; thermosetting plastics harden permanently when cured and cannot be resoftened
optionC: Thermoplastics are stronger than thermosetting plastics
optionD: Thermosetting plastics are cheaper and more widely used
explanation: Thermoplastics soften on heating and can be reshaped repeatedly (e.g. acrylic; PVC). Thermosetting plastics undergo a permanent chemical change on curing and cannot be remoulded (e.g. epoxy resin; urea formaldehyde).

text: What is acrylic (PMMA) classified as?
optionA: A thermosetting plastic
optionB: A thermoplastic
optionC: A ferrous metal
optionD: A composite material
explanation: Acrylic (Perspex/PMMA — polymethyl methacrylate) is a thermoplastic: it can be bent and shaped when heated. Common uses include display signs; windows and CNC-cut products.

text: What is MDF (Medium Density Fibreboard)?
optionA: A type of ferrous metal
optionB: A manufactured board made from compressed wood fibres bound with resin
optionC: A type of thermoplastic
optionD: A naturally grown hardwood
explanation: MDF is a manufactured board made by compressing dried wood fibres with synthetic resin binder under heat. It has consistent properties; no grain; and is easy to machine but susceptible to moisture.

text: What is the main difference between hardwood and softwood?
optionA: Hardwood is always harder than softwood
optionB: Hardwood comes from deciduous (broad-leaved) trees; softwood from coniferous (cone-bearing) trees
optionC: Softwood always has a finer grain than hardwood
optionD: Hardwood is cheaper than softwood
explanation: The classification refers to the type of tree: hardwoods from deciduous trees (oak; mahogany); softwoods from conifers (pine; spruce). Some softwoods can be harder than some hardwoods by density.

text: What is a ferrous metal?
optionA: A metal that never rusts
optionB: A metal that contains iron as its main component
optionC: A metal that is always non-magnetic
optionD: A metal derived from a plant source
explanation: Ferrous metals contain iron. Examples include mild steel; cast iron; stainless steel. Most ferrous metals are magnetic and susceptible to corrosion except stainless steel.

text: What is a composite material?
optionA: A material made from a single pure element
optionB: A material made from two or more distinct materials combined to give properties neither has alone
optionC: A material that can be recycled indefinitely
optionD: A material found only in nature
explanation: Composites combine materials to exploit their complementary properties: GRP (glass fibre + polyester resin) is strong; light and corrosion-resistant; Kevlar is bulletproof yet flexible.

text: What is a smart material?
optionA: A material with a fixed and predictable property
optionB: A material that changes its properties in response to an external stimulus such as temperature; light or stress
optionC: A material used only in computing
optionD: A material that is cheaper than conventional alternatives
explanation: Smart materials respond to stimuli: thermochromic materials change colour with temperature; shape memory alloys return to a preset shape; piezoelectric materials generate voltage under stress.

text: What is the purpose of annealing a metal?
optionA: To harden and strengthen it
optionB: To relieve internal stresses and soften the metal; making it more workable
optionC: To add a protective surface coating
optionD: To join two metal pieces together
explanation: Annealing involves heating a metal to a specific temperature and cooling slowly. This relieves work-hardening stresses; restoring ductility and making the metal easier to cut; bend or machine.

text: What advantage do manufactured boards such as plywood and MDF have over solid timber?
optionA: They are always stronger in every direction
optionB: They are available in large flat sheets; are more dimensionally stable and have no natural grain direction weaknesses
optionC: They are lighter than all solid woods
optionD: They never absorb moisture
explanation: Manufactured boards are made in large consistent sheets; free from knots; with no dominant grain direction (so equal strength all round) — advantages over natural solid timber.

text: What does the term 'work hardening' mean when applied to metals?
optionA: Heating a metal to change its grain structure
optionB: A process where repeated cold working (bending; hammering) increases the hardness and brittleness of a metal
optionC: Applying a protective coating to prevent corrosion
optionD: A type of welding process
explanation: Work hardening occurs when a metal is repeatedly deformed at room temperature (e.g. bending copper back and forth). Dislocations in the crystal structure increase; making it harder and more brittle.

text: What is injection moulding?
optionA: Pouring liquid plastic into an open mould
optionB: Forcing molten thermoplastic under pressure into a closed mould where it cools and solidifies
optionC: Heating a flat plastic sheet and pressing it into a former with a vacuum
optionD: Spinning molten plastic on a rotating former
explanation: Injection moulding injects molten thermoplastic at high pressure into a closed steel mould; producing complex accurate shapes quickly. Used for mass-produced components: bottle caps; phone cases.

text: What is the difference between soldering and brazing?
optionA: There is no difference — they are the same process
optionB: Soldering uses a low-temperature filler (below ~450°C); brazing uses a higher-temperature filler (above ~450°C); both join metals without melting the parent material
optionC: Brazing is used only on plastics; soldering only on metals
optionD: Soldering uses an electric arc; brazing uses an oxy-acetylene torch
explanation: Both soldering and brazing join metals using a molten filler that bonds on cooling. Soldering uses tin-based solder (melting point <450°C); brazing uses brass or silver alloys at higher temperatures.

text: What type of joint is a mortise and tenon?
optionA: A temporary knock-down joint
optionB: A permanent wood joint where a rectangular projection (tenon) fits into a corresponding slot (mortise)
optionC: A type of metal welded joint
optionD: A type of plastic fusion joint
explanation: The mortise and tenon is a classic permanent wood joint: the tenon (rectangular projection on one piece) fits into the mortise (rectangular hole in the other); often glued for permanence.

text: What does CNC stand for in manufacturing?
optionA: Computer Numerical Control
optionB: Creative Network Construction
optionC: Carbon Non-Combustible
optionD: Component and Nominal Code
explanation: CNC (Computer Numerical Control) machines are controlled by computer programs; allowing precise; repeatable cutting; milling; turning or engraving without manual operation.

text: What are knock-down (KD) fittings used for?
optionA: Permanently joining parts that cannot be separated
optionB: Temporarily joining furniture panels so they can be assembled and disassembled without special tools
optionC: Welding two metal pieces at high temperature
optionD: Reinforcing stressed joints in a structure
explanation: KD fittings (cam locks; scan fittings; two-piece corner blocks) allow flat-pack furniture to be assembled by the user without tools and disassembled for transport or storage.

text: What is electroplating?
optionA: A type of plastic moulding process
optionB: A finishing process that deposits a thin layer of metal onto a surface using electrolysis
optionC: A type of heat treatment for steel
optionD: A method of sharpening cutting tools
explanation: Electroplating passes an electric current through an electrolyte solution; depositing metal ions onto the workpiece surface. Used for corrosion resistance (chrome plating) or appearance.

text: What does a laser cutter do in CAM?
optionA: It drills holes by spinning a sharp drill bit
optionB: It uses a focused high-power laser beam to cut or engrave materials controlled by a computer design file
optionC: It bends metal sheets to precise angles using a hydraulic press
optionD: It applies a painted finish to surfaces
explanation: A laser cutter focuses a high-energy laser beam onto a material; vaporising or melting it along a path defined by a CAD file. Used for cutting; engraving wood; acrylic; card; some metals.

text: What is the purpose of a risk assessment before using machinery?
optionA: To slow down work and add paperwork
optionB: To identify hazards; evaluate the risk of harm; and put in place controls to reduce or eliminate the risk
optionC: To provide evidence for the examiner
optionD: To replace safety equipment in the workshop
explanation: A risk assessment identifies what could cause harm; how likely it is and how severe; then specifies controls (guards; PPE; training; procedures) to manage those risks.

text: What is PPE?
optionA: Personal Practical Equipment
optionB: Personal Protective Equipment — clothing and devices worn to protect against specific hazards
optionC: A type of safety certification for products
optionD: A programming language used in CAM
explanation: PPE (Personal Protective Equipment) includes safety goggles; gloves; ear defenders; dust masks and aprons worn to protect against eye injury; cuts; noise; fumes and dust.

text: Why should loose clothing and long hair be tied back when using machinery?
optionA: For aesthetic reasons only
optionB: To prevent clothing or hair being caught in rotating parts; which could cause serious injury
optionC: Because it is a school uniform requirement
optionD: Because it improves the quality of the finished work
explanation: Loose clothing and unrestrained hair can be drawn into rotating machinery (drills; lathes; grinders); causing serious injury. Securing them removes this entanglement hazard.

text: What does the warning symbol of a skull and crossbones indicate on a material?
optionB: Toxic or poisonous — the material is harmful or fatal if inhaled; swallowed or absorbed through the skin
optionC: Flammable — keep away from naked flames
optionD: Corrosive — will damage skin and eyes on contact
answer: Explosive — may detonate if exposed to heat
difficulty: The skull and crossbones (GHS06) is the standard hazard symbol for acute toxicity — the material is poisonous if inhaled; ingested or contacts skin.

text: What must a designer consider about safety when designing a product for children?
optionA: Only the colour and aesthetics
optionB: That the product must be free from sharp edges; small parts that could cause choking; toxic materials and sharp points
optionC: That children prefer bright primary colours
optionD: That the product must be as cheap as possible to manufacture
explanation: Designers have a legal and ethical responsibility for user safety. Children's products must comply with safety standards: no sharp edges; no small detachable parts (choking hazard); non-toxic materials; tested to relevant standards.

text: Before using a pillar drill; which safety check should ALWAYS be performed?
optionA: Check the colour of the material being drilled
optionB: Check that the work is securely clamped and the guard is in place
optionC: Check that the drill bit matches the colour of the material
optionD: Check that there are other people watching to assist
explanation: Before drilling: the workpiece must be clamped (not held by hand) to prevent spinning; the guard must be positioned and the chuck key removed before starting.

text: What is the purpose of a machine guard?
optionA: To improve the appearance of the machine
optionB: To prevent accidental contact with moving or dangerous parts of the machine during operation
optionC: To increase the speed of the machine
optionD: To hold the workpiece in position
explanation: Guards are physical barriers that prevent operators from accidentally touching blades; rotating parts or other dangerous elements while the machine is running.

text: Why is it important to maintain and store sharp cutting tools correctly?
optionA: Because they look better when properly stored
optionB: Because dull or badly stored tools require more force to use; increasing the risk of slipping and causing injury
optionC: Because new tools are expensive
optionD: Because clean tools are easier to photograph for the portfolio
explanation: Dull tools require excessive force; making them more likely to slip and cause cuts. Correct storage (edge guards; racks) prevents both blunting and accidental contact with sharp edges.

text: What does a strut do in a structure?
optionA: It is a member under tension
optionB: It is a structural member that resists compressive (pushing) forces along its length
optionC: It is a surface that resists bending only
optionD: It is a decorative element in a frame
explanation: A strut is a compression member — it resists being shortened by forces along its axis. Examples: columns; legs of a table; the top chord of a truss.

text: What does a tie do in a structure?
optionA: It is a member under compression
optionB: It is a structural member that resists tensile (pulling) forces — it is being stretched
optionC: It is a member that resists twisting
optionD: It is a waterproof coating applied to steel
explanation: A tie is a tension member — it is stretched by forces along its axis. Examples: the bottom chord of a roof truss; suspension bridge cables; guy wires.

text: What is triangulation used for in structures?
optionA: To join plastic components with glue
optionB: To add rigidity to a frame by using triangular bracing — triangles cannot be deformed without changing side lengths
optionC: To measure angles in a building
optionD: To create aesthetic patterns in architectural designs
explanation: A triangle is the only polygon that cannot change shape without changing its side lengths. Adding diagonal bracing to rectangular frames creates triangles; making the structure rigid.

text: What is a moment in structural terms?
optionA: A measurement of time in a construction project
optionB: The turning effect of a force about a pivot point; calculated as Force × Perpendicular Distance (Nm)
optionC: The speed at which a structure can be built
optionD: A type of joint used in steel construction
explanation: A moment (or torque) is the tendency of a force to cause rotation about a point. Moment = Force (N) × perpendicular distance from the pivot (m); unit: Nm.

text: What does tension mean when applied to a structural member?
optionA: The member is being compressed (shortened)
optionB: The member is being stretched; with forces pulling at both ends
optionC: The member is being twisted
optionD: The member is bending in the middle
explanation: Tension occurs when equal and opposite forces pull a member from both ends; stretching it. Steel cables in a suspension bridge are in tension.

text: What does compression mean in structural terms?
optionA: Forces pulling a member apart
optionB: Forces pushing inwards on a member; tending to shorten it
optionC: A force that causes twisting
optionD: A force that causes bending without any axial load
explanation: Compression occurs when equal and opposite forces push inward on a member; tending to shorten it. Columns in a building carry compressive loads from the floors above.

text: What is the Factor of Safety in structural design?
optionA: The percentage of profit made when manufacturing
optionB: A multiplier applied to the calculated working load to account for uncertainties; ensuring the structure can bear more than expected loads
optionC: The ratio of hardwood to softwood in a frame
optionD: A measurement of a material's colour fastness
explanation: Factor of Safety = Ultimate load / Working load. A factor of 2 means the structure is designed to hold twice the expected load — this provides a safety margin for unexpected forces.

text: What is a gusset plate used for?
optionA: To reduce the weight of a structure
optionB: To reinforce joints in a frame by distributing forces over a larger area
optionC: To provide a smooth finish to a metallic surface
optionD: To measure angles in a truss
explanation: A gusset plate is a flat piece of metal or wood used at joints to connect members; spreading forces over a larger area and preventing the joint from deforming.

text: What is mechanical advantage (MA)?
optionA: The ratio of velocity to force in a mechanism
optionB: The ratio of load to effort — how much a mechanism multiplies the input force
optionC: The number of moving parts in a mechanism
optionD: The speed ratio between input and output
explanation: Mechanical Advantage = Load / Effort. An MA > 1 means the mechanism magnifies the input force (e.g. a lever lifting a heavy load with less force than its weight).

text: What is a first-class lever?
optionA: A lever where the effort is between the fulcrum and the load
optionB: A lever where the fulcrum is between the effort and the load
optionC: A lever where the load is between the fulcrum and the effort
optionD: A lever with no fulcrum
explanation: In a first-class lever; the fulcrum is between the effort and the load — the lever arm reverses direction. Examples: a seesaw; scissors; a crowbar.

text: What does a gear ratio tell you?
optionA: The colour code of a gear wheel
optionB: The relationship between the rotational speeds (or turns) of two meshing gears — determined by their number of teeth
optionC: The material a gear is made from
optionD: How much torque a motor produces
explanation: Gear ratio = teeth on driven gear / teeth on driving gear. If the driven gear has more teeth; it spins slower but with more torque (and vice versa).

text: What type of motion does a crankshaft convert?
optionA: Rotary to linear and linear to rotary
optionB: Linear to oscillating only
optionC: Oscillating to reciprocating only
optionD: Linear to rotary only
explanation: A crankshaft (and crank-slider mechanism) converts rotary motion to reciprocating (back-and-forth) linear motion; or vice versa. Used in engines; pumps and sewing machines.

text: What is reciprocating motion?
optionA: Motion in a continuous circular path
optionB: Motion that goes back and forth in a straight line
optionC: Motion that swings from side to side about a fixed point
optionD: Motion that only moves in one direction
explanation: Reciprocating motion is linear back-and-forth movement (e.g. the piston of an engine; a saw blade; a sewing machine needle).

text: What is oscillating motion?
optionA: Back-and-forth linear motion along a straight line
optionB: A swinging or rocking motion about a fixed pivot point (like a pendulum)
optionC: Continuous circular rotation
optionD: One-directional linear motion
explanation: Oscillating motion swings about a fixed point: a pendulum; a metronome arm and a rocking chair all oscillate. It differs from reciprocating (purely linear back-and-forth).

text: What is a cam mechanism used for?
optionA: To join two shafts at right angles
optionB: To convert rotary motion into reciprocating or varying linear motion via a follower
optionC: To increase the torque of a motor
optionD: To measure the speed of a rotating shaft
explanation: A cam is a specially shaped rotating component; as it rotates; a follower riding on its surface moves up and down (or in/out) in a pattern determined by the cam profile.

text: What is a worm gear used for?
optionA: Transmitting motion between two parallel shafts
optionB: Transmitting motion between two shafts at right angles with a large speed reduction and high torque multiplication
optionC: Connecting two shafts that are in-line
optionD: Increasing shaft speed with a small torque reduction
explanation: A worm gear (worm and worm wheel) produces a large gear reduction in a compact space; transmitting motion between perpendicular (90°) shafts. The worm can drive the wheel but not vice versa (self-locking).

text: What does Ohm's Law state?
optionA: Voltage = Current × Capacitance
optionB: Voltage = Current × Resistance (V = I × R)
optionC: Current = Resistance × Voltage
optionD: Resistance = Voltage × Current
explanation: Ohm's Law: V = I × R (Voltage = Current × Resistance). This can be rearranged: I = V/R (current = voltage ÷ resistance) or R = V/I.

text: What happens to the total resistance when two resistors are connected in series?
optionA: Total resistance is the average of the two values
optionB: Total resistance equals the sum of both resistances (R_total = R1 + R2)
optionC: Total resistance is less than the smallest resistor
optionD: Total resistance equals R1 × R2
explanation: In series; resistances add: R_total = R1 + R2 + ... (+ more). The same current flows through each resistor.

text: A circuit has a 9V battery and a resistor of 180Ω. What current flows through the circuit?
explanation: Using Ohm's Law: I = V ÷ R = 9 ÷ 180 = 0.05 A (50 mA).

text: What is an LDR (Light Dependent Resistor)?
optionA: A resistor whose value changes with temperature
optionB: A resistor whose resistance decreases as the light level on it increases
optionC: A device that emits light when current passes through it
optionD: A capacitor that stores charge in proportion to light intensity
explanation: An LDR (photoresistor) has high resistance in darkness and low resistance in bright light. Used in circuits that respond to light levels (e.g. automatic night lights; burglar alarms).

text: What is a thermistor?
optionA: A device that always has a fixed resistance
optionB: A component whose resistance changes with temperature (usually decreasing as temperature increases for an NTC thermistor)
optionC: A type of transistor used for switching
optionD: A device that converts heat into electricity
explanation: An NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) thermistor has high resistance when cold and low resistance when hot. Used in temperature-sensing circuits and thermostats.

text: What is the function of a transistor in a switching circuit?
optionA: It converts AC to DC
optionB: A small current into the base turns on a much larger current flowing between collector and emitter — acting like an electronically controlled switch
optionC: It stores charge and releases it slowly
optionD: It converts resistance into voltage
explanation: In switching mode; a small base current allows a larger collector-emitter current to flow. When base current stops; the collector-emitter path is open (off). Used to switch loads from low-power sensor circuits.

text: What does the 555 timer IC do in an astable configuration?
optionA: It stores data until it is switched off
optionB: It produces a continuous square wave output — repeatedly switching between high and low — without any external trigger
optionC: It acts as a one-shot pulse (fires once then stops)
optionD: It measures the frequency of an input signal
explanation: In astable mode; the 555 continuously oscillates (on/off); generating a square wave. The frequency and duty cycle depend on external resistors and a capacitor. Used in LED flashers; alarms; tone generators.

text: What is a potential divider circuit used for in electronics?
optionA: To divide electric current into equal parts
optionB: To produce a variable output voltage from a fixed supply voltage; proportional to the ratio of two resistors
optionC: To double the supply voltage
optionD: To filter AC from a DC circuit
explanation: A potential divider uses two resistors in series across a supply. The voltage at the junction between them = Vs × R2/(R1+R2). Used with LDRs/thermistors to give a voltage that changes with light/temperature.

text: What is a diode used for in an electronic circuit?
optionA: To amplify small signals
optionB: To allow current to flow in one direction only; acting as a one-way valve for current
optionC: To store charge and release it slowly
optionD: To measure voltage in a circuit
explanation: A diode conducts current in its forward-biased direction (anode to cathode) and blocks it in reverse. Used in rectifiers; protection circuits and flyback diodes across relay coils.

text: What is the purpose of including a resistor in series with an LED?
optionA: To increase the brightness of the LED
optionB: To limit the current through the LED; protecting it from burning out
optionC: To reverse-bias the LED and prevent it from conducting
optionD: To increase the voltage across the LED
explanation: LEDs have a forward voltage drop of about 1.8–3V and must have current limited (typically 10–20 mA). A series resistor of R = (Vs − Vf) / If is calculated and fitted to prevent excess current destroying the LED.

text: What is the difference between an input device and an output device?
optionA: Input devices display information; output devices capture it
optionB: Input devices send data into a computer; output devices transmit processed data from the computer to the outside world
optionC: Input devices use power; output devices do not
optionD: Input devices are connected by wire; output devices by wireless
explanation: Input devices (keyboard; mouse; camera) feed data into the computer. Output devices (monitor; printer; speaker) deliver processed results from the computer to the user.

text: Which of the following is an OUTPUT device?
optionA: Keyboard
optionB: Scanner
optionC: Monitor
optionD: Microphone
explanation: A monitor displays processed data from the computer — it is an output device. Keyboard; scanner and microphone are all input devices.

text: What type of device is a touchscreen?
optionA: An input device only
optionB: An output device only
optionC: Both an input and an output device
optionD: Neither an input nor an output device
explanation: A touchscreen is both: the screen (output) displays information; and the touch-sensitive surface (input) detects the user's touch and sends position data to the computer.

text: What is the function of a scanner?
optionA: To print documents
optionB: To capture a physical image or document and convert it to digital data
optionC: To display images from the computer
optionD: To process audio signals
explanation: A scanner converts a physical document or image into a digital file by capturing reflected light from the surface and converting it to pixel data.

text: What is an actuator in a computer control system?
optionA: A sensor that detects conditions
optionB: An output device that physically does something in response to a signal (e.g. motor; heater; valve; LED)
optionC: A type of input device for data entry
optionD: A programming language for robotics
explanation: An actuator is an output device that converts a signal into physical action: motors; solenoids; heaters; LEDs and valves are all actuators in control systems.

text: What does a barcode reader do?
optionA: It prints barcodes on products
optionB: It converts the pattern of light and dark bars in a barcode into a digital code that the computer can process
optionC: It stores barcodes in a database
optionD: It encodes text into a barcode format
explanation: A barcode reader uses a laser or image sensor to detect the light/dark pattern of a barcode; then converts this into a numerical code that is sent to the computer (e.g. for stock control or checkout).

text: What is a sensor in a computer control system?
optionA: A device that displays output to the user
optionB: A device that detects a physical condition (temperature; light; pressure) and sends a corresponding signal to the computer
optionC: A device that processes data
optionD: A device that stores programs
explanation: Sensors detect physical stimuli (temperature; light; pressure; proximity; sound) and convert them into electrical signals that a computer can read and act upon.

text: What type of output does a speaker produce?
optionA: Visual output (images)
optionB: Tactile output (vibration felt by touch)
optionC: Audio output (sound waves)
optionD: Data output to a network
explanation: Speakers convert electrical audio signals from the computer into sound waves — they produce audio output.
